elements.quote: The findings highlighted the need for country-specific analysis for malaria control optimization, the use of country-specific epidemiological and cost data in performing modelling analyses, performing cost sensitivity analyses and defining the perspective for the analysis, with an emphasis on subnational tailoring for data collection and analysis for more accurate and good quality results. It is critical that the future modelling efforts account for fairness and target at risk malaria populations that are hard-to-reach to maximize impact.

elements.quote: Background Despite advances made in curbing the global malaria burden since the 2000s, progress has stalled, in part due to a plateauing of the financing available to implement needed interventions. In 2020, approximately 3.3 billion USD was invested globally for malaria interventions, falling short of the targeted 6.8 billion USD set by the GTS, increasing the financial gap between desirable and actual investment.
elements.reason: The abstract describes the current state of knowledge (progress has stalled; financing shortfall) and thus frames important uncertainties relevant to optimisation models for malaria control.

elements.quote: Models for malaria control optimization are used to disentangle the most efficient interventions or packages of interventions for inherently constrained budgets. This systematic review aimed to identify and characterise models for malaria control optimization for resource allocation in limited resource settings and assess their strengths and limitations.
elements.reason: The abstract explicitly states the rationale and importance of the review (need to identify and characterise models to inform resource allocation under constrained budgets) and explains why the review is needed.
No evidence was found in the provided text that discusses existing similar systematic reviews, cites previous reviews, or explains why this review is needed as an update or replication.

elements.quote: Models for malaria control optimization are used to disentangle the most efficient interventions or packages of interventions for inherently constrained budgets.
elements.reason: The review focuses on models for optimisation of malaria control rather than being a review of intervention effects; therefore describing mechanisms of action of interventions is not applicable to this review.

elements.quote: This systematic review aimed to identify and characterise models for malaria control optimization for resource allocation in limited resource settings and assess their strengths and limitations.
elements.reason: No logic model or discussion of hypothesised relationships between intervention components and outcomes is expected or provided because the review concerns optimisation models rather than evaluation of complex intervention delivery; thus the logic-model requirement is not applicable.

elements.quote: This systematic review aimed to identify and characterise models for malaria control optimization for resource allocation in limited resource settings and assess their strengths and limitations.
elements.reason: The abstract contains an explicit statement of the review aim and objectives, clearly describing the review question to identify and characterise models for malaria control optimization and assess their strengths and limitations.

The review addresses identification and characterisation of optimization models rather than estimating effects of interventions; it is not a review of intervention effects requiring PICO-formulated planned comparisons.

elements.quote: Each record in the search were included if they met all of the following criteria: (1) Were scientific peer-reviewed journals written in English; (2) Were published before 30th June 2024; (3) Studies were included irrespective of the targeted geographical regions; (4) Studies were included irrespective of the population subgroups; (5) Studies containing an optimization model (mathematical or statistical); (6) All studies with human Plasmodium species; (7) Studies with two or more interventions; (8) Cost data were used in combination with the model outputs; (9) Outcomes/health benefits were clearly stated and/or measured.
elements.reason: The manuscript lists multiple study characteristics used for eligibility (language, date, region, population, presence of optimization model, Plasmodium species, number of interventions, cost data, outcomes). It does not explicitly specify eligible study designs in depth (beyond 'scientific peer-reviewed journals') or any follow-up requirements, so the element is only partially satisfied.

elements.quote: A narrative synthesis of the study characteristics was performed. ... There is a marked heterogeneity across all studies in the optimization modelling analyses used to. Specifically, as some studies use dynamic transmission models [16, 17, 28, 32], individual-based models [18, 25, 33-35, 37], or decision tree models [10, 11], the disparities in these optimization modelling analyses across studies make the comparison of the methods used to measure outcomes across these studies difficult.
elements.reason: The authors describe heterogeneity qualitatively and identify factors (e.g., model type, data sources, administrative level) and note a narrative synthesis was used, but they do not describe specific informal methods or structured approaches (with factor levels) used to explore heterogeneity in detail.

elements.quote: This manuscript provides a systematic review of existing literature to identify models for malaria control optimization. However, the review has certain limitations, which are outlined below: The review did not include abstracts from scientific conferences or other scientific meetings, potentially omitting important modelling studies conducted by national malaria control programs (NMCPs) to inform resource allocation decisions. And so, although the findings from this review shows that there are relatively few published modelling studies or examples that incorporate cost constraints and describe how to optimize limited budgets, the findings from this manuscript may not fully represent the actual use of models for malaria control optimization worldwide. The absence of these studies from the review limits the comprehensiveness of the findings, suggesting a need for the development of additional approaches to better capture and reflect the full range of modelling activities being undertaken globally.
